questions.explanation: 'Will' marks a characteristic or habitual behaviour, often with a note of disapproval.
questions.q: Even after all these years, he ___ leave his wet towels on the bedroom floor.

questions.explanation: 'Would' describes a repeated action in the past; it expresses a past habit, not a one-off event.
questions.q: When we were children, my grandmother ___ bake bread every Sunday morning.

questions.explanation: 'Won't' expresses present unwillingness or refusal to perform an action.
questions.q: I've asked him three times, but he simply ___ help with the move.

questions.explanation: 'If you will' in a conditional conveys willingness rather than a future event.
options: If you will just listen for a minute
questions.q: Choose the sentence that expresses a request for someone's cooperation.

questions.explanation: 'Would' softens an invitation into polite indirectness, unlike the blunter 'will'.
options: Would you care to join us for dinner?
Will you care to join us for dinner?
Do you join us for dinner?
You join us for dinner, will you?
questions.q: Choose the most polite, formal invitation.

questions.explanation: With inanimate subjects, 'will/won't' describes characteristic function or failure, not choice.
questions.q: The old printer ___ print double-sided, no matter which driver you install.

questions.explanation: 'Would' with stative verbs of feeling in the past can signal a repeated emotional habit.
questions.q: Whenever the meeting dragged on, she ___ feel her patience wearing thin.

questions.explanation: 'Will' in the main clause after 'if' expresses a characteristic habit of the subject.
questions.q: If you press that nerve, he ___ every time — it's just how he reacts.

questions.explanation: A firm 'I will' after a doubt states determination and willingness, not merely future time.
options: I shall have seen it through
I would have seen it through
questions.q: Choose the sentence showing firm determination to finish the project.

questions.explanation: 'Won't' reports a persistent refusal, stronger than simple present 'doesn't'.
questions.q: The committee ___ approve any budget that lacks a full audit trail.

questions.explanation: 'Would always' recalls a habitual past trait, whereas 'will always' states a general truth.
questions.q: As a boy he ___ lose his keys and blame his sister.

questions.explanation: The bare imperative plus 'will you' softens a command into a request.
questions.q: Choose the most polite way to ask someone to open the window.

questions.explanation: 'Would' can describe a past willingness that was repeatedly shown, not a single offer.
questions.q: She ___ take credit for the team's work; modesty was her habit.

questions.explanation: In first-conditional threats, 'will' in the if-clause signals a stubborn habit the speaker resents.
questions.q: Choose the sentence with a tone of irritation at someone's repeated behaviour.

questions.explanation: 'Would' marks habitual past behaviour; the present perfect 'has done' is wrong with a finished past period.
questions.q: Back in those days, he ___ ten minutes early, without exception.

questions.explanation: 'Will not be told' is a refusal to accept instruction; 'is not told' is merely a fact.
questions.q: He ___ told what to write — he resigns first.

questions.explanation: 'Will' with weather or natural subjects describes a characteristic tendency, not volition.
questions.q: English weather ___ change its mind by the afternoon.

questions.explanation: 'Wouldn't' in the past reports refusal then; 'won't' would report refusal now.
questions.q: She offered him the promotion, but he ___ accept it.

questions.explanation: Only the 'would' version is a conditional request; the others are statements.
options: Do you lend me your notes?
Would you lend me your notes?
Lend me your notes, shall you?
questions.q: Choose the correct polite request.

questions.explanation: 'Will' expresses a prediction based on characteristic behaviour, not a scheduled event.
questions.q: Give him an inch and he ___ take a mile — that's his nature.
